topics.name: Luminosity
topics.kicker: A star’s total power output · How bright it truly is, not how bright it looks
topics.briefing: Luminosity is the total amount of energy a star gives off every second: its true power output. The Sun’s luminosity is about 380 trillion trillion watts. A star can look faint just because it is far away, so astronomers keep luminosity separate from apparent brightness, which depends on distance. Stars whose luminosity is known, like Cepheid variables, work as “standard candles” for measuring the universe.
topics.answerHtml: Luminosity (prompt on brightness or power; do not accept “apparent brightness” or “magnitude”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: If a star’s surface temperature doubles while its size stays the same, this quantity becomes 16 times larger, because the Stefan–Boltzmann law says it grows with the fourth power of temperature. It also grows with the square of a star’s radius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the total amount of energy a star gives off every second.

tossups.p: While measuring stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, Henrietta Swan Leavitt found that Cepheid [“SEF-ee-id”] variables that take longer to brighten and dim have greater values of this quantity. Her 1912 discovery later let Edwin Hubble show that the Andromeda “nebula” is a separate galaxy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, a star’s total power output, often given in units of the Sun’s.

tossups.p: In the Morgan–Keenan system, Roman numerals give a star’s “class” named for this quantity, from I for supergiants down to V for main-sequence dwarfs. The V at the end of the Sun’s label, G2V, comes from that scheme.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the total energy a star gives off per second, measured in watts.

tossups.p: Arthur Eddington found a limit on this quantity: above it, the outward push of a star’s own light, called radiation pressure, becomes stronger than the star’s gravity and drives gas away from the star.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the total power given off by a star or another glowing object, measured in watts.

tossups.p: For main-sequence stars, this quantity rises roughly as mass to the 3.5 power, so a star ten times as massive as the Sun has thousands of times the Sun’s value, while a star with half the Sun’s mass has less than a tenth of it.
tossups.r: That is why the most massive stars burn out in only a few million years. For 10 points, name this measure of a star’s total power output.

tossups.p: Carl Sagan and George Mullen pointed out a puzzle: early in Earth’s history, the Sun had only about 70 percent as much of this quantity as it has in modern times, yet young Earth still had liquid water. That puzzle is called the faint young Sun paradox.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the total energy the Sun or another star gives off each second.

tossups.p: Dividing this quantity by 4π times the square of a star’s distance gives the flux that we measure on Earth, a rule called the inverse-square law. Astronomers who know both the flux and this quantity for a star can work out how far away it is.
tossups.r: Because of that rule, a powerful star can still look faint if it is far away. For 10 points, name this quantity, a star’s true total power output.

tossups.p: In 1998, two teams compared the known peak value of this quantity for Type Ia supernovae with how faint those explosions looked, and discovered that the universe’s expansion is speeding up. Objects with a known value of this quantity are called standard candles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of the total energy an object gives off per second.

tossups.p: Multiplying the solar constant, about 1,361 watts per square meter, by 4π times the square of Earth’s distance from the Sun gives the Sun’s value of this quantity, about 3.8 × 10²⁶ watts.
tossups.r: Astronomers often give it for other stars in units of the Sun’s value. For 10 points, name this quantity, a star’s total power output.

tossups.p: Many white dwarfs are hotter than the Sun but have far less of this quantity because they are so small, while cool red giants have much more of it because they are so huge. The red supergiant Betelgeuse [“BEE-tul-jooz”] has an enormous value of this quantity despite its cool surface.
tossups.r: Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell plotted it against temperature. For 10 points, name this total power output of a star.

tossups.p: A star’s absolute magnitude, which is how bright it would look from 10 parsecs away, is a backward, logarithmic stand-in for this quantity: a star whose absolute magnitude is five lower has 100 times more of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the total energy a star gives off each second, measured in watts.

tossups.p: Astronomers call this quantity “bolometric” when it counts energy at every wavelength, a term that comes from the bolometer, a heat-measuring device invented by Samuel Langley. Visible light makes up only part of the Sun’s total.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, a star’s total power output, which is often compared to the Sun’s.

tossups.p: Sirius is the brightest star in our night sky mostly because it is only about 8.6 light-years away; it has only about 25 times the Sun’s value of this quantity. Rigel [“RYE-jul”] looks fainter, but it has more than a thousand times as much of this quantity as Sirius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, a star’s true power output, as opposed to how bright it looks from Earth.

tossups.p: The distance from a star to its habitable zone, where a planet could have liquid water, grows with the square root of this quantity. Most red dwarfs have so little of it that their habitable zones lie closer in than Mercury’s orbit around the Sun.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of the total energy a star gives off per second.

tossups.p: Quasars, which are powered by gas falling into supermassive black holes, have some of the highest values of this quantity in the universe, often more than all the stars in their home galaxies put together, even though that glow comes from a region only a few light-days across.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the total power an object gives off, often measured in watts.

Along the main sequence it rises with mass, so hot, blue, massive stars give off the most

Morgan–Keenan classes named for it use Roman numerals: I = supergiants, III = giants, V = main-sequence dwarfs (the Sun is G2V)

The solar constant (about 1,361 watts per square meter) times 4π times Earth’s distance squared gives the Sun’s value, about 3.8 × 10²⁶ watts
“Bolometric” means counted over all wavelengths, after the bolometer, a heat-measuring device invented by Samuel Langley
In 1998, Type Ia supernovae used as standard candles showed that the universe’s expansion is speeding up
The distance to a star’s habitable zone grows with the square root of this value; most red dwarfs’ habitable zones are closer to them than Mercury is to the Sun
Betelgeuse (a red supergiant) and Rigel give off enormous amounts; Rigel looks fainter than Sirius but gives off over a thousand times as much
Quasars, powered by supermassive black holes, can give off more than all the stars in their home galaxies combined
Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell first plotted it against temperature (about 1911–1913)
Edwin Hubble used Leavitt’s Cepheids in the 1920s to show that the Andromeda “nebula” is a separate galaxy

trap.title: True power or apparent brightness?
trap.body: Luminosity is a star’s true power output, but how bright a star looks from Earth, its apparent brightness or flux, also depends on how far away it is. Absolute magnitude and apparent magnitude are different quantities that rate brightness on a backward, logarithmic scale. Players who hear “bright” clues often blurt out “brightness” or “magnitude” instead of the exact term.
trap.fix: Watts, units of the Sun’s output, the Stefan–Boltzmann law, Leavitt’s Cepheids, the Eddington limit, and “total energy per second” all mean luminosity. “As seen from Earth,” “divided by distance squared,” or “watts per square meter” mean flux; a number on a scale where lower means brighter is a magnitude.
trap.line: Real answer line: Luminosity (prompt on brightness or power; do not accept “apparent brightness” or “magnitude”)

topics.name: Asteroids
topics.kicker: Rocky leftovers of the early solar system · Most orbit between Mars and Jupiter
topics.briefing: Asteroids are rocky, airless leftovers from the birth of the solar system, and most of them circle the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. They range from boulders to Ceres, which is about 940 kilometers across. One asteroid’s impact 66 million years ago helped wipe out the dinosaurs, so in 2022 NASA tested a defense: it crashed its DART spacecraft into a small asteroid and changed its orbit.
topics.answerHtml: Asteroids (accept asteroid belt or minor planets; do not accept “comets” or “meteors”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss became famous for working out the orbit of the first of these objects after it vanished into the Sun’s glare, so that astronomers could find it again. Giuseppe Piazzi [“pee-AHT-see”] had spotted that object from Palermo, Sicily, on January 1, 1801, the first night of the 19th century.
tossups.r: That object is Ceres. For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, most of which orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.

tossups.p: Heinrich Olbers, who found two of the earliest of these objects, suggested that they were pieces of a planet that had broken apart. William Herschel named them from a Greek word meaning “star-like,” because even through a telescope they looked like tiny points of light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, which are found mostly in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.

tossups.p: Daniel Kirkwood noticed gaps in this region where an object’s orbit would match up evenly with Jupiter’s, such as circling the Sun exactly three times for every one orbit of Jupiter. Jupiter’s repeated tugs have cleared out those lanes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this region of rocky bodies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

tossups.p: One of these objects, Dinkinesh, turned out to have a tiny moon when a NASA probe named for a famous fossil skeleton flew past it in 2023. That probe, Lucy, launched in 2021 to visit groups of these objects that travel ahead of and behind Jupiter in its orbit.
tossups.r: Most of these objects orbit between Mars and Jupiter, but the Trojans share Jupiter’s orbit. For 10 points, name these rocky bodies.

tossups.p: On September 26, 2022, NASA deliberately crashed its DART spacecraft into Dimorphos [“dye-MOR-fus”], the small moon of one of these objects, Didymos [“DID-ih-mos”]. The crash shortened Dimorphos’s orbit by about 32 minutes, the first test of a way to protect Earth from impacts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, one of which helped wipe out the dinosaurs.

tossups.p: Luis and Walter Alvarez found a thin clay layer rich in iridium, a metal that is rare in Earth’s crust but more common in these objects, and argued in 1980 that one of them had struck Earth. The crater it left, Chicxulub [“CHEEK-shoo-loob”], lies buried under Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, one of which helped end the age of dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

tossups.p: Japan’s Hayabusa [“hah-yah-BOO-sah”] probe brought back the first sample from one of these objects, Itokawa, in 2010. In 2023, a capsule from NASA’s OSIRIS-REx parachuted into the Utah desert carrying rocks and dust from another one, Bennu.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, most of which orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.

tossups.p: One of these objects, Vesta, has a giant crater with one of the tallest mountains in the solar system at its center, and it is the brightest of these objects in our sky. NASA’s Dawn probe used ion engines to orbit Vesta and then Ceres.
tossups.r: Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth. For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, whose largest member, Ceres, is also called a dwarf planet.

tossups.p: In 1991, the Galileo spacecraft made the first close flyby of one of these objects, Gaspra, on its way to Jupiter. Two years later, Galileo photographed another one, Ida, and revealed the first known moon of one of these objects, a little body later named Dactyl.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, most of which lie in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.

tossups.p: In 2001, the NEAR Shoemaker probe became the first spacecraft to land on one of these objects, Eros, after orbiting it for a year. Eros, discovered in 1898, was the first of these objects found that comes close to Earth’s orbit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, some of which are called near-Earth objects.

tossups.p: In 2004, one of these objects named for an Egyptian serpent of chaos briefly reached level 4 on the Torino [“tuh-REE-noh”] scale of impact danger, the highest rating given to any object as of 2025. That object, Apophis [“uh-POF-iss”], will safely pass closer to Earth than some satellites on April 13, 2029.
tossups.r: Many of these objects are watched closely because their orbits come near Earth’s. For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, most of which orbit between Mars and Jupiter.

tossups.p: Astronomers sort these objects by their colors and spectra into dark, carbon-rich C-types, which are the most common, stony S-types, and metal-rich M-types. In 2023, NASA launched a probe named Psyche toward a metal-rich one of these objects with the same name.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, most of which orbit between Mars and Jupiter.

tossups.p: In February 2013, one of these objects about 20 meters wide exploded high above Chelyabinsk [“chel-YAH-binsk”], Russia, and its shock wave shattered windows across the city. A yearly awareness day about these objects is held on June 30, the anniversary of a bigger 1908 blast over Tunguska, Siberia.
tossups.r: These objects are larger than meteoroids but smaller than planets. For 10 points, name these rocky bodies, most of which orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.

tossups.p: A rule called the Titius–Bode law predicted a missing planet between Mars and Jupiter, so astronomers formed a search team nicknamed the “Celestial Police.” Members of that team found three of these objects, Pallas, Juno, and Vesta, between 1802 and 1807.
tossups.r: Ceres, found in 1801, came first. For 10 points, name these rocky bodies of the inner solar system.

tossups.p: Pioneer 10 became the first spacecraft to cross this region, in 1972 and 1973, and many probes have flown through it since without hitting anything, because its objects are spread so far apart. All of them together have only a few percent of the mass of Earth’s Moon.
tossups.r: Jupiter’s gravity kept its objects from ever forming a planet. For 10 points, name this region of rocky bodies between Mars and Jupiter.

trap.title: Asteroid, comet, or meteor?
trap.body: Asteroids get mixed up with icy comets and with meteors, the streaks of light made when small bits of space rock burn up in Earth’s air. A piece smaller than about a meter is a meteoroid, and one that reaches the ground is a meteorite. Ceres is another trap: it is the biggest object in the asteroid belt, but it is also a dwarf planet with an answer line of its own.
trap.fix: Rocky or metal bodies between Mars and Jupiter, the Trojans, Kirkwood gaps, DART, and sample-return missions like Hayabusa and OSIRIS-REx mean asteroids. A coma or a tail means comets; a streak of light in the sky means a meteor. If the question says “these objects,” give the whole group, not Ceres or Vesta.
trap.line: Real answer line: Asteroids (accept asteroid belt or minor planets; do not accept “comets” or “meteors”)

topics.name: Mercury (planet)
topics.kicker: Smallest planet and closest to the Sun · A year lasts only 88 days
topics.dates: Known since ancient times; first visited by Mariner 10 in 1974
topics.briefing: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, racing around it in just 88 days. With almost no air to trap heat, its days reach about 430°C (800°F) and its nights drop to about −180°C (−290°F). Yet ice hides in craters near its poles, where sunlight never reaches. It also spins so slowly that one sunrise-to-sunrise day there lasts about 176 Earth days.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1965, Gordon Pettengill and Rolf Dyce bounced radar signals off this planet from the Arecibo [“air-uh-SEE-boh”] telescope and found that it spins once about every 59 days. Until then, astronomers had thought it always kept the same face toward the Sun.
tossups.r: It is named for the Roman messenger god. For 10 points, name this smallest planet, the closest one to the Sun.

tossups.p: Urbain Le Verrier [“luh-vair-YAY”] blamed a tiny extra drift in this planet’s orbit on an unseen inner planet he called Vulcan. In 1915, Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity explained that drift, about 43 arcseconds per century, without any extra planet.
tossups.r: This planet’s year lasts only about 88 Earth days. For 10 points, name this innermost planet of the solar system.

tossups.p: On the exact opposite side of this planet from its giant Caloris Basin lies jumbled “weird terrain,” which was probably shaken up by shock waves from the impact that made the basin. Caloris gets its name from the Latin word for heat, because it lies at one of this planet’s hottest spots.
tossups.r: Mariner 10 saw only half of that basin. For 10 points, name this heavily cratered planet, the smallest and closest to the Sun.

tossups.p: Mariner 10 became the first spacecraft to use one planet’s gravity to swing toward another when it flew past Venus on its way to this planet in 1974. On three flybys, Mariner 10 mapped less than half of this planet’s surface.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this small, cratered planet, the closest to the Sun, which no spacecraft visited again until MESSENGER.

tossups.p: In 2015, a probe crashed into this planet after running out of fuel, ending four years in orbit. That probe, MESSENGER, the first spacecraft to orbit this planet, had confirmed in 2012 that water ice lies in craters near its poles where sunlight never reaches.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, which has the shortest year in the solar system, about 88 Earth days.

tossups.p: A European and Japanese mission launched in 2018 is named for Giuseppe “Bepi” Colombo, who explained why this planet spins exactly three times for every two orbits. That mission, BepiColombo, flew past this planet six times between 2021 and 2025.
tossups.r: This planet is named for the speedy Roman messenger god. For 10 points, name this innermost planet.

tossups.p: MESSENGER found bright, shallow pits called hollows on this planet, which may form as some material in its rocks turns to gas and escapes. With almost no atmosphere to hold in heat, its days reach about 430 degrees Celsius, while its nights plunge to about minus 180 degrees.
tossups.r: Even so, Venus is hotter, because of its thick atmosphere. For 10 points, name this planet, the closest to the Sun.

tossups.p: From some spots on this planet, the Sun seems to rise, stop, back up, and then rise again. Because of the way its spin and orbit combine, one full day from sunrise to sunrise there lasts about 176 Earth days, twice as long as its year.
tossups.r: It has no moons. For 10 points, name this smallest planet, whose year lasts about 88 Earth days.

tossups.p: Long, curving cliffs called lobate scarps cross this planet’s surface; they formed as the whole planet shrank while its huge iron core cooled. That core takes up about 85 percent of this planet’s radius.
tossups.r: This planet is the second-densest after Earth. For 10 points, name this planet, the smallest in the solar system.

tossups.p: In 1631, Pierre Gassendi [“gah-sahn-DEE”] became the first person to watch this planet cross in front of the Sun, as Johannes Kepler had predicted. Those crossings, called transits, happen only in May or November, such as one on November 11, 2019.
tossups.r: This planet never strays far from the Sun in our sky. For 10 points, name this innermost planet.

tossups.p: In Gustav Holst’s orchestral suite _The Planets_, the third movement calls this planet “the Winged Messenger.” The French word for Wednesday, “mercredi,” comes from the god for whom this planet is named.
tossups.r: That god is the Roman counterpart of Hermes. For 10 points, name this planet, the closest to the Sun.

tossups.p: This planet has the most stretched-out orbit of any planet, swinging between about 46 million and 70 million kilometers from the Sun. It is also the fastest-moving planet, racing around the Sun at an average of about 47 kilometers per second.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, whose year lasts only about 88 Earth days.

tossups.p: A 2019 calculation showed that, averaged over time, this planet, not Venus, is the closest planet to Earth, because it never wanders far from the Sun. On average, it is also the closest planet to every other planet.
tossups.r: It is only slightly larger than Earth’s Moon. For 10 points, name this smallest planet, the innermost in the solar system.

tossups.p: Mariner 10 surprised scientists by finding that this planet has a magnetic field, about one percent as strong as Earth’s. Sunlight pushes sodium atoms out of this planet’s extremely thin atmosphere, called an exosphere, into a long tail like a comet’s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, which has no moons and is the closest to the Sun.

tossups.p: Craters on this planet are named for famous artists, writers, and composers, such as Beethoven and Rembrandt, while its long cliffs are named for ships of exploration, such as Discovery and Endeavour.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this heavily cratered planet, which looks a lot like Earth’s Moon and is the closest to the Sun.

clues.t: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun
The shortest year of any planet: one orbit takes about 88 Earth days
Named for the speedy Roman messenger god, the counterpart of the Greek Hermes
Heavily cratered, so it looks a lot like Earth’s Moon; it has no moons of its own
Almost no atmosphere, so its days reach about 430°C (800°F) and its nights drop to about −180°C (−290°F)
Venus is hotter, even though it is farther from the Sun, because of its thick greenhouse atmosphere
The Caloris Basin is one of the solar system’s largest impact basins; “Caloris” comes from the Latin for heat
Mariner 10 (1974–1975) was its first visitor, after the first-ever gravity assist, from Venus
MESSENGER, the first spacecraft to orbit it (2011–2015), confirmed water ice in shadowed craters near its poles
Spins exactly three times for every two orbits around the Sun (a 3:2 resonance)
Einstein’s general relativity (1915) explained the extra drift, or precession, of its orbit: about 43 arcseconds per century
A huge iron core, about 85 percent of its radius, makes it the second-densest planet after Earth
One solar day, from sunrise to sunrise, lasts about 176 Earth days, as long as two of its years
It crosses the Sun’s face in transits, which happen only in May or November (one was on November 11, 2019)
Gordon Pettengill and Rolf Dyce found with Arecibo radar in 1965 that it spins about once every 59 days; it had been thought to keep one face to the Sun
Urbain Le Verrier blamed its orbit’s drift on an unseen inner planet he called Vulcan
Giuseppe “Bepi” Colombo explained its 3:2 spin; the European–Japanese BepiColombo mission (launched 2018) is named for him
“Weird terrain” on the side opposite the Caloris Basin was probably jumbled by the impact’s shock waves
Long cliffs called lobate scarps formed as the whole planet shrank while its core cooled
MESSENGER found bright, shallow pits called hollows, which may form as material in the rocks turns to gas
Its craters are named for artists, writers, and composers, such as Beethoven and Rembrandt
Its long cliffs are named for ships of exploration, such as Discovery and Endeavour
Pierre Gassendi watched the first observed transit, in 1631, as Johannes Kepler had predicted
From some spots on its surface, the Sun seems to rise, stop, back up, and then rise again
The most stretched-out (eccentric) orbit of any planet, about 46 to 70 million km from the Sun, and the fastest planet, about 47 km per second
A 2019 calculation found that, on average, it is the closest planet to Earth, and to every other planet
Mariner 10 found a weak magnetic field (about 1 percent of Earth’s); sunlight pushes sodium from its exosphere into a comet-like tail
Holst’s _The Planets_ calls it “the Winged Messenger”; the French “mercredi” (Wednesday) comes from its god

trap.title: Planet, god, or Venus?
trap.body: Mercury is also the Roman messenger god (the Greek Hermes) and the name of a liquid metal, so cross-category clues about the god can pull players off the planet. In astronomy, Mercury and Venus are both inner planets with no moons that show phases and cross the Sun’s face in transits, so those clues alone do not settle which one is meant.
trap.fix: The 88-day year, the 3:2 spin, the Caloris Basin, Mariner 10, MESSENGER, BepiColombo, and Einstein’s 43-arcsecond drift mean Mercury. Acid clouds, a runaway greenhouse effect, a backward spin, Venera, and Magellan mean Venus. If the question says “this planet,” name the planet even when a clue mentions the messenger god.

topics.name: Exoplanets
topics.kicker: Planets that orbit other stars · More than 5,000 confirmed as of 2025
topics.dates: First confirmed 1992; first around a Sun-like star 1995
topics.briefing: Exoplanets are planets that orbit stars other than the Sun. The first ones were confirmed in 1992, circling the leftover core of an exploded star, and as of 2025 astronomers had confirmed more than 5,000. Most are found indirectly, by spotting a star that dims slightly when a planet passes in front of it, or that wobbles as a planet tugs on it. Some are scorching gas giants; a few might have liquid water.

tossups.p: In 2015, a pulsar was officially named Lich, and the three of these objects circling it were named Draugr, Poltergeist, and Phobetor. In 1992, Aleksander Wolszczan [“VOHL-shchahn”] and Dale Frail had made the first confirmed discovery of these objects around that pulsar.
tossups.r: Most of these objects circle ordinary stars instead. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars other than the Sun.

tossups.p: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz [“kuh-LOH”] shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for finding one of these objects in 1995 that circles the star 51 Pegasi every four days. That gas giant, the first of these objects found around a Sun-like star, orbits so close that it is called a hot Jupiter.
tossups.r: Mayor and Queloz found it by the wobble it causes in its star. For 10 points, name these planets found beyond our solar system.

tossups.p: When a planet the size of Jupiter crosses in front of a star like the Sun, the star dims by about one percent; an Earth-sized planet dims it by less than one-hundredth of a percent. From 2009 to 2013, a space telescope stared at one patch of sky in the constellations Cygnus and Lyra to catch such dips.
tossups.r: That telescope, Kepler, found thousands of these objects using the transit method. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars other than the Sun.

tossups.p: The radial velocity method finds these objects by watching a star’s light shift back and forth toward red and blue as the star wobbles, an example of the Doppler effect. That method gives only a minimum value for each object’s mass.
tossups.r: That method found the first of these objects around a Sun-like star, in 1995. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars beyond the Sun.

tossups.p: In 2017, astronomers announced that a cool red dwarf star about 40 light-years away, TRAPPIST-1, has seven Earth-sized examples of these objects, all orbiting closer to their star than Mercury is to the Sun.
tossups.r: Several of them lie in the star’s habitable zone, where liquid water could exist. For 10 points, name these planets that circle stars other than our Sun.

tossups.p: Kepler-186f, announced in 2014, was the first Earth-sized one of these objects found at just the right distance from its star, where liquid water could exist on its surface. That object is slightly larger than Earth and orbits a red dwarf star.
tossups.r: Astronomers call that just-right region the “Goldilocks zone,” or habitable zone. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars other than our Sun.

tossups.p: In 2016, the Pale Red Dot campaign found one of these objects, Proxima Centauri b, orbiting the closest star to the Sun, about 4.2 light-years away. That object is probably a little more massive than Earth.
tossups.r: It lies in its star’s habitable zone, where liquid water could exist. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars other than the Sun.

tossups.p: Kepler-16b was nicknamed “Tatooine” after Luke Skywalker’s home world, because it circles a pair of stars that also orbit each other. That planet, announced in 2011, is a cold gas giant with about the mass of Saturn.
tossups.r: NASA’s TESS satellite was launched in 2018 to search most of the sky for more of these objects. For 10 points, name these planets beyond our solar system.

tossups.p: In 1999, HD 209458 b became the first of these objects seen passing in front of its star. The Hubble Space Telescope later detected sodium in that object’s atmosphere, the first atmosphere found on one of these objects.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these planets that circle stars other than the Sun.

tossups.p: In 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope made the first clear detection of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of one of these objects, a hot gas giant called WASP-39b. Webb reads such atmospheres from starlight that filters through them as the planets pass in front of their stars.
tossups.r: Webb was launched on December 25, 2021. For 10 points, name these planets found outside our solar system.

tossups.p: Combining how much one of these objects dims its star with how much it makes the star wobble lets astronomers find its density, which shows whether it is rocky or gassy. Hot Jupiters, gas giants that orbit their stars in just a few days, were among the first of these objects found.
tossups.r: Their tight orbits make them easy to spot by the wobble they cause. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars other than the Sun.

tossups.p: In 2008, astronomers released direct pictures of three giant examples of these objects circling the star HR 8799, and a fourth was spotted two years later. Most of these objects are far too faint to photograph next to their bright stars.
tossups.r: Most others are found indirectly instead, by watching their stars dim or wobble. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars other than the Sun.

tossups.p: In gravitational microlensing, the gravity of a passing star bends and briefly brightens the light of a more distant star, and a tiny extra spike in that light can reveal one of these objects. Microlensing can even find rogue ones drifting through space with no star at all.
tossups.r: That method relies on the bending of light that Albert Einstein predicted. For 10 points, name these planets beyond our solar system.

tossups.p: In 2015, the International Astronomical Union let the public help name some of these objects, and 51 Pegasi b became Dimidium [“dih-MID-ee-um”], Latin for “half,” because its mass is about half of Jupiter’s. Such objects are labeled with lowercase letters, starting with “b.”
tossups.r: Most have only catalog names, like Kepler-16b or TRAPPIST-1e. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars other than the Sun.

tossups.p: Super-Earths and mini-Neptunes, which are bigger than Earth but smaller than Neptune, are among the most common kinds of these objects that astronomers have found, yet our solar system has none. Studies suggest that most stars in our galaxy have planets of their own.
tossups.r: As of 2025, more than 5,000 had been confirmed. For 10 points, name these planets that orbit stars other than the Sun.

trap.title: Exoplanet or a look-alike?
trap.body: Exoplanet tossups often lead with something else in the system. The first confirmed exoplanets orbit a pulsar, so players who hear “Wolszczan” may blurt out “pulsar.” Brown dwarfs are failed stars, too heavy to count as planets, and an exomoon would be a moon of an exoplanet. Saying just “planets” earns a prompt, so be ready to add “exo-.”
trap.fix: Listen for “these objects” or “these planets” plus the methods (transit, radial velocity, microlensing) and missions (Kepler, TESS, Webb). Those mean exoplanets, even when the first clue names the star they orbit, like a pulsar, 51 Pegasi, or TRAPPIST-1.
trap.line: Real answer line: Exoplanets (accept extrasolar planets; prompt on planets)

topics.name: Venus (planet)
topics.kicker: Hottest planet in the solar system · Earth’s cloudy, scorching twin
topics.dates: Known since ancient times; first visited by Mariner 2 in 1962
topics.briefing: Venus is almost the same size as Earth, but it is the hottest planet in the solar system, even hotter than Mercury, with a surface temperature of about 465°C (870°F). Its thick carbon dioxide air traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect and presses down more than 90 times as hard as Earth’s air. It also spins backward, so slowly that one rotation takes longer than its year.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1982, the Soviet lander Venera 13 took the first color photos of this planet’s surface and lasted 127 minutes in the crushing heat. Twelve years earlier, Venera 7 had become the first spacecraft to send back data from the surface of another planet when it landed here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this second planet from the Sun, the hottest planet in the solar system.

tossups.p: In 1610, Galileo saw this planet go through a full set of phases, from a thin crescent to nearly full, much like the Moon. Ptolemy’s Earth-centered model could not explain those phases, so they supported Copernicus’s idea that the planets orbit the Sun.
tossups.r: It is often called the Morning Star or the Evening Star. For 10 points, name this planet, the brightest one in the night sky.

tossups.p: James Cook sailed to Tahiti in 1769 to time a rare event in which this planet crosses in front of the Sun, a measurement meant to reveal the Sun’s distance. The next pair of such events is due in 2117 and 2125.
tossups.r: Those transits come in pairs eight years apart, such as 2004 and 2012. For 10 points, name this planet, the second from the Sun.

tossups.p: Jeremiah Horrocks was the first person known to watch this planet pass in front of the Sun, in 1639. During a later transit in 1761, Mikhail Lomonosov [“luh-muh-NOH-sof”] saw a glowing ring around this planet and concluded that it has an atmosphere.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, sometimes called Earth’s twin because of its similar size.

tossups.p: Nearly every feature on this planet is named for a woman, real or mythical; one exception is its tallest mountain range, Maxwell Montes, named for physicist James Clerk Maxwell. NASA’s Magellan orbiter mapped nearly all of this planet with radar in the early 1990s.
tossups.r: Magellan used radar because thick clouds hide this planet’s surface. For 10 points, name this planet, the second from the Sun.

tossups.p: Raised regions on this planet named Ishtar Terra and Aphrodite Terra honor goddesses of love from Babylonian and Greek myth. This planet also has ring-shaped features called coronae [“kuh-ROH-nee”] and flat-topped volcanic mounds nicknamed “pancake domes.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, whose surface is hidden by thick clouds of sulfuric acid.

tossups.p: This planet spins backward compared with most planets, so the Sun rises in the west there. It spins so slowly that one rotation takes about 243 Earth days, longer than the 225 days it takes to orbit the Sun.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet with no moons, the second from the Sun.

tossups.p: Winds at the cloud tops of this planet whip all the way around it in about four Earth days, far faster than the planet itself turns. At the surface, the air presses down about 92 times as hard as on Earth, like being nearly a kilometer deep in the ocean.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, whose thick carbon dioxide atmosphere makes it the hottest in the solar system.

tossups.p: In 1962, NASA’s Mariner 2 made the first successful flyby of another planet when it passed this one and measured its scorching temperature. Japan’s Akatsuki orbiter missed its first try at entering orbit around this planet in 2010, but it succeeded in 2015.
tossups.r: Its clouds reflect so much sunlight that it shines brighter than any other planet. For 10 points, name this planet, the hottest in the solar system.

tossups.p: Ancient Greeks once thought this planet was two different objects: Phosphorus, which rose before the Sun, and Hesperus, which appeared after sunset. It can shine so brightly that it casts faint shadows on very dark nights.
tossups.r: It is named for the Roman goddess of love. For 10 points, name this planet, often called the Morning Star and the Evening Star.

tossups.p: Gustav Holst’s _The Planets_ calls this planet “the Bringer of Peace,” and the French word for Friday, “vendredi,” comes from this planet’s Latin name. Its astronomical symbol, a circle above a small cross, is also used as the symbol for female.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, named for the Roman goddess of love and beauty.

tossups.p: Carl Sagan argued in the early 1960s that heat trapped by this planet’s thick atmosphere explained why radio telescopes measured it as so hot. Its surface is hot enough to melt lead, and as of 2025 no lander there had lasted much more than two hours.
tossups.r: That runaway greenhouse effect, caused by carbon dioxide, makes it the hottest planet. For 10 points, name this planet, which is hotter than Mercury even though it is farther from the Sun.

tossups.p: In 2020, a team led by Jane Greaves announced that they had detected phosphine, a gas that might hint at life, high in this planet’s clouds, but other scientists have challenged the finding. Those clouds are made of droplets of sulfuric acid.
tossups.r: Its thick carbon dioxide air makes it the hottest planet. For 10 points, name this second planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: The Maya tracked this planet’s 584-day cycle of appearances in careful tables preserved in the Dresden Codex, and Babylonian astronomers recorded its risings and settings on clay tablets. Like Mercury, it never strays far from the Sun in our sky.
tossups.r: It is usually seen in the morning or evening sky. For 10 points, name this planet, the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon.

tossups.p: In 2023, scientists found a volcanic vent on this planet that had changed shape between radar images taken eight months apart in 1991, strong evidence of an active volcano. That vent lies on Maat Mons, this planet’s tallest volcano.
tossups.r: This planet is close to Earth in size and mass. For 10 points, name this planet, often called Earth’s twin.

trap.title: Planet, goddess, or painting?
trap.body: Venus shares its name with the Roman goddess of love (the Greek Aphrodite) and with Botticelli’s painting _The Birth of Venus_, which are separate answer lines. In astronomy, Venus and Mercury are both inner planets that show phases and cross the Sun’s face in transits, and players who assume the closest planet must be the hottest sometimes say Mercury on “hottest planet” clues.
trap.fix: Thick sulfuric-acid clouds, a runaway greenhouse effect, the hottest surface, a backward spin, Venera, Magellan, and Maxwell Montes mean Venus. The 88-day year, the Caloris Basin, MESSENGER, and Einstein’s 43-arcsecond drift mean Mercury. If the question says “this planet,” name the planet, even when a clue mentions the goddess.

topics.name: Titan (moon)
topics.kicker: Saturn’s largest moon · The only moon with a thick atmosphere
topics.briefing: Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, is bigger than the planet Mercury and is the only moon wrapped in a thick atmosphere. Under its orange haze, methane falls as rain and fills rivers, lakes, and seas, making it the only world besides Earth known to have liquid on its surface. In 2005, Europe’s Huygens probe parachuted down to its frozen ground, the most distant landing ever made as of 2025.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1944, Gerard Kuiper [“KY-per”] found methane on this world, making it the first moon known to have an atmosphere. The air at its surface presses down about one and a half times as hard as Earth’s air does.
tossups.r: That air is mostly nitrogen. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Saturn.

tossups.p: Pictures from the surface of this moon showed rounded pebbles, probably made of water ice, like stones on a riverbed. The lander that took them had parachuted down through this moon’s orange haze for more than two hours.
tossups.r: That lander, Huygens, touched down on January 14, 2005. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Saturn.

tossups.p: Christiaan Huygens [“HOY-gunz”] discovered this moon in 1655, the first new moon found since Galileo spotted four around Jupiter in 1610. It was also the first moon ever found circling Saturn.
tossups.r: In 1847, John Herschel named it for the generation of gods that included Cronus. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Saturn.

tossups.p: Kraken Mare, the largest sea on this moon, and its other seas are named for sea monsters, such as Ligeia [“lih-JEE-uh”] and Punga. Cassini’s radar first spotted lakes there in 2006, mostly near this moon’s north pole.
tossups.r: Those seas hold liquid methane and ethane. For 10 points, name this moon, the only world besides Earth known to have stable liquid on its surface.

tossups.p: A bright region the size of Australia on this moon is named Xanadu, after the summer capital of Kublai Khan described in Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s poem “Kubla Khan.” The Hubble Space Telescope first spotted Xanadu through this moon’s haze in 1994, using infrared light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this hazy moon of Saturn, the second-largest moon in the solar system.

tossups.p: To get a close look at this moon in 1980, Voyager 1 took a path that flung it up out of the plane of the planets, so it could not go on to visit Uranus or Neptune. Even so, Voyager 1’s cameras could not see through this moon’s thick orange haze.
tossups.r: That haze surrounds the only moon with a thick atmosphere. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Saturn.

tossups.p: In 2019, NASA chose Dragonfly, a car-sized drone with eight rotors, to explore this moon by flying from place to place, which is easier there because of the thick air and weak gravity. Dragonfly is designed to study chemistry that might lead to life.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this moon of Saturn, where the Huygens probe landed in 2005.

tossups.p: On this moon, a cycle much like Earth’s water cycle runs on methane instead: clouds of methane drop rain that carves river channels and fills lakes. The surface is about minus 180 degrees Celsius, so cold that water ice is as hard as rock.
tossups.r: It is the second-largest moon in the solar system. For 10 points, name this moon of Saturn, which has a thick nitrogen atmosphere.

tossups.p: This moon is wider than the planet Mercury but has less than half of Mercury’s mass, because it is about half ice. It circles its planet about once every 16 days, always keeping the same face toward it.
tossups.r: Only Jupiter’s Ganymede [“GAN-ih-meed”] is a bigger moon. For 10 points, name this largest moon of Saturn.

tossups.p: Cassini found that this moon flexes as it orbits Saturn, which suggests that a salty ocean of liquid water lies deep beneath its icy crust. Dunes made of grains of organic material ripple across the region around its equator.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this moon with a thick nitrogen atmosphere, the largest of Saturn’s.

tossups.p: Sunlight breaks apart methane high in this moon’s air, and the pieces join into orange, smog-like particles called tholins [“THOH-linz”], a name coined by Carl Sagan. Those particles slowly drift down onto the ground below.
tossups.r: This moon was discovered by Christiaan Huygens in 1655. For 10 points, name this hazy moon, the largest of Saturn’s.

tossups.p: Mountains on this moon are named for mountains in J. R. R. Tolkien’s Middle-earth, and its lakes are named for lakes on Earth. One of them, Ontario Lacus [“LAH-kus”], is about the size of Lake Ontario.
tossups.r: Most of its seas lie near its north pole. For 10 points, name this moon of Saturn with lakes of liquid methane.

tossups.p: The Cassini spacecraft flew past this moon more than 100 times, using its gravity to change course, and a final “goodbye kiss” flyby in April 2017 sent Cassini on its last orbits before it plunged into Saturn.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this largest moon of Saturn, which has a thick atmosphere.

tossups.p: Saturn’s lumpy moon Hyperion is locked in a rhythm with this larger moon, circling three times for every four of its orbits. On Christmas Day 2004, the Cassini spacecraft released a probe that landed on this moon about three weeks later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this moon, the only one in the solar system with a thick atmosphere.

tossups.p: Because Saturn takes about 29 and a half years to orbit the Sun, each season on this moon lasts more than seven Earth years, and Cassini watched spring arrive in its north. Scientists study its smoggy haze for clues to chemistry like that of the very early Earth.
tossups.r: It is bigger than the planet Mercury. For 10 points, name this moon of Saturn, which has seas of liquid methane.

trap.title: Moon, Titans, or Triton?
trap.body: Titan is named for the Titans, the generation of Greek gods that included Cronus, and “Titans” is a separate mythology answer line. In astronomy, players mix up Titan with Triton, Neptune’s largest moon, and with Titania, Uranus’s largest moon. And when a Saturn question describes Titan, the answer is the planet, not the moon.
trap.fix: Saturn, Huygens, Cassini, Kraken Mare, methane lakes, a thick nitrogen atmosphere, and Dragonfly mean Titan. A backward orbit, nitrogen geysers, and Voyager 2 in 1989 mean Triton; Shakespeare’s fairy queen and Uranus mean Titania. If the question says “this moon,” answer “Titan,” not “Titans.”

topics.name: Pulsars
topics.kicker: Spinning neutron stars · Cosmic lighthouses that tick like clocks
topics.briefing: In 1967, graduate student Jocelyn Bell noticed a radio signal that ticked every 1.3 seconds, so regular that her team jokingly nicknamed it LGM-1, for “Little Green Men.” It was the first pulsar: a spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radio waves across space like a lighthouse. Some pulsars spin hundreds of times a second and keep time so steadily that astronomers use them as cosmic clocks.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While checking long paper charts from a radio telescope she had helped build, a Cambridge graduate student noticed a bit of “scruff” that turned out to be a signal repeating every 1.3 seconds. Her team jokingly labeled it LGM-1, for “Little Green Men.”
tossups.r: That student, Jocelyn Bell, had found the first of these objects. For 10 points, name these spinning neutron stars that give off regular pulses of radio waves.

tossups.p: Antony Hewish shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics, the first ever given for astronomy, for his role in the discovery of these objects, but his student who first noticed them was left out. In 2018, that student won a three-million-dollar Breakthrough Prize and gave all of it to fund physics scholarships.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rapidly spinning neutron stars, the first of which Jocelyn Bell found in 1967.

tossups.p: Inside the Crab Nebula, the wreck of a star that Chinese astronomers saw explode in 1054 CE, one of these objects spins about 30 times every second. The energy it loses as it slowly spins down keeps the whole nebula glowing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rotating neutron stars that sweep beams across space like lighthouses.

tossups.p: In 1974, Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor used the Arecibo [“air-uh-SEE-boh”] telescope to find one of these objects orbiting another neutron star. The pair’s slowly shrinking orbit matched Albert Einstein’s prediction of gravitational waves, earning a 1993 Nobel Prize.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these spinning neutron stars that give off regular radio pulses.

tossups.p: The plaques on Pioneer 10 and 11 and the covers of the Voyager Golden Records show where the Sun is by using a map of 14 of these objects, with each one’s rhythm written in binary code.
tossups.r: That map was meant to show any finders where the spacecraft came from. For 10 points, name these rapidly rotating neutron stars that act like cosmic lighthouses.

tossups.p: Some of these objects are “recycled” when gas pulled from a partner star spins them up. As of 2025, the fastest known one, in the star cluster Terzan 5, spun 716 times every second.
tossups.r: Such fast spinners are called millisecond examples of these objects. For 10 points, name these spinning neutron stars that emit regular pulses.

tossups.p: These objects send out beams from their magnetic poles, which are tilted away from the axis they spin around. In 1968, Thomas Gold explained how they work, and his idea was confirmed when one in the Crab Nebula was found to be slowly losing spin.
tossups.r: Each beam sweeps past Earth like a lighthouse’s. For 10 points, name these spinning neutron stars, the first of which Jocelyn Bell found in 1967.

tossups.p: In 1992, Aleksander Wolszczan [“VOHL-shchahn”] and Dale Frail found the first confirmed planets outside the solar system orbiting one of these objects. Tiny changes in the timing of its pulses revealed the planets’ tugs.
tossups.r: These objects are left behind when massive stars explode as supernovae. For 10 points, name these rapidly spinning neutron stars.

tossups.p: In 2023, the NANOGrav team announced evidence of a low hum of gravitational waves filling the universe, found by timing dozens of these objects for 15 years. The pulses of some of these objects arrive so steadily that they rival atomic clocks.
tossups.r: These objects are the leftover cores of exploded stars. For 10 points, name these spinning neutron stars, which act like cosmic lighthouses.

tossups.p: The Vela supernova remnant holds one of these objects that spins about 11 times a second and sometimes suddenly speeds up in events called glitches. Those glitches may happen when a superfluid deep inside the star suddenly shifts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rotating neutron stars that send out regular pulses of radio waves.

tossups.p: The cover of Joy Division’s 1979 album _Unknown Pleasures_ shows dozens of stacked radio signals from the first of these objects ever found, CP 1919. That object’s pulses repeat about every 1.3 seconds.
tossups.r: It was found in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell. For 10 points, name these spinning neutron stars, which tick like cosmic clocks.

tossups.p: “Black widow” examples of these objects blast their small partner stars with so much radiation and wind that they slowly evaporate them. Black widows are millisecond examples of these objects, spun up by gas they had earlier pulled from that same partner.
tossups.r: These objects send out beams that sweep past Earth like a lighthouse’s. For 10 points, name these rapidly spinning neutron stars.

tossups.p: Free electrons in space slow down the lower radio frequencies of these objects’ pulses, so astronomers use that delay, called dispersion, to estimate how far away each one is. Their catalog names begin with the letters PSR.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these objects, rotating neutron stars that sweep beams of radio waves past Earth.

tossups.p: Most of these objects slowly lose spin as they turn their rotational energy into radiation and fast-moving particles, so an older one usually turns more slowly than a young one. Eventually they spin too slowly for their beams to keep shining.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these spinning neutron stars, the first of which was found in 1967.

tossups.p: In 1971, the Uhuru satellite caught Centaurus X-3, one of these objects that pulls in gas from a partner star, ticking in X-rays. In 2017, an experiment on the International Space Station showed that X-ray signals from these objects could guide spacecraft, like a cosmic GPS.
tossups.r: Most of these objects are seen in radio waves. For 10 points, name these spinning neutron stars that pulse like lighthouses.

trap.title: Pulsar, neutron star, or quasar?
trap.body: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars, but not every neutron star is seen as a pulsar, and “Neutron stars” is a separate answer line. On a pulsar question, saying “neutron star” earns a prompt; on a neutron star question, saying “pulsar” is wrong. Quasars sound alike but are something else entirely: blazing disks of gas around supermassive black holes in faraway galaxies.
trap.fix: Regular ticks, the lighthouse beam, LGM-1, the Crab’s 30 spins a second, millisecond timing, and the Hulse–Taylor binary mean pulsars. If the clues describe the whole family of super-dense collapsed stars (Baade and Zwicky, the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit), say neutron stars. Galaxy-outshining glows and black holes mean quasars.
trap.line: Real answer line: Pulsars (accept pulsar; prompt on neutron stars)

topics.name: Uranus
topics.kicker: Seventh planet, tipped on its side · First planet found with a telescope
topics.briefing: Uranus is the planet that rolls around the Sun on its side: its axis is tipped about 98 degrees, so each pole gets about 42 years of sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness. William Herschel spotted it from his garden in Bath, England, in 1781, making it the first planet found with a telescope. This icy, blue-green giant has thin, dark rings and moons named mostly for characters from Shakespeare.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: John Flamsteed recorded this planet in 1690 but mistook it for a star, which he labeled 34 Tauri. When this planet’s true discoverer first saw it, he reported it as a comet.
tossups.r: William Herschel found it from his garden in Bath, England, in 1781. For 10 points, name this seventh planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: This planet’s discoverer wanted to name it Georgium Sidus, or “George’s Star,” to honor King George III, who rewarded him with a yearly salary. Johann Bode [“BOH-duh”] instead suggested the name we use for it, which finally caught on everywhere around 1850.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet discovered by William Herschel, the seventh from the Sun.

tossups.p: In 1789, Martin Klaproth named a newly found element after this planet, which had been discovered just eight years earlier. The next element on the periodic table is named for the next planet farther from the Sun.
tossups.r: This planet is named for the Greek god of the sky, the father of Cronus. For 10 points, name this seventh planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: In 1977, astronomers on a flying observatory watched a star blink off and on several times before and after this planet passed in front of it, revealing a set of thin, dark rings.
tossups.r: James Elliot’s team had found the second ring system known in the solar system. For 10 points, name this seventh planet, which is tipped on its side.

tossups.p: Each pole of this planet gets about 42 years of nonstop sunlight followed by about 42 years of darkness. A giant collision long ago may explain why this planet is tipped so far over.
tossups.r: Its axis is tilted about 98 degrees, so it spins on its side. For 10 points, name this seventh planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: In January 1986, Voyager 2 made the only spacecraft visit to this planet as of 2025, finding several new moons and measuring its day at about 17 hours. During that flyby, this planet’s south pole pointed almost straight at the Sun.
tossups.r: That spacecraft flew on to Neptune in 1989. For 10 points, name this blue-green ice giant, the seventh planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: Verona Rupes, a cliff on this planet’s moon Miranda, is estimated to be about 20 kilometers tall, probably the tallest cliff in the solar system. Miranda’s patchwork surface looks as if the moon had been broken apart and stuck back together.
tossups.r: Miranda was discovered by Gerard Kuiper in 1948. For 10 points, name this planet, whose moons are named for characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

tossups.p: In 1787, this planet’s discoverer found its two largest moons, Titania and Oberon, which are named for the queen and king of the fairies in _A Midsummer Night’s Dream_. William Lassell found two more, Ariel and Umbriel, in 1851.
tossups.r: Voyager 2 found several more of its moons in 1986. For 10 points, name this seventh planet, discovered by William Herschel.

tossups.p: This planet has the coldest atmosphere of any planet, dipping to about minus 224 degrees Celsius, partly because, unlike its outer neighbor, it gives off almost no extra heat from inside.
tossups.r: Methane in its air gives it a blue-green color. For 10 points, name this ice giant, the seventh planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: Alexis Bouvard [“boo-VAR”] published tables of this planet’s motion in 1821, but it kept drifting off course, so he suspected that an unseen planet was tugging on it. That hidden planet, Neptune, was found in 1846.
tossups.r: Its discoverer was William Herschel. For 10 points, name this planet, the seventh from the Sun.

tossups.p: Voyager 2 found that this planet’s magnetic field is tipped nearly 60 degrees from its spin axis and is centered far from the middle of the planet. Its moons and rings circle around its sharply tilted equator.
tossups.r: Like Neptune, this planet is called an ice giant. For 10 points, name this planet that spins on its side.

tossups.p: This planet’s discoverer earned his living as a musician and church organist in Bath, England, and he ground the mirrors for his own telescopes. He composed symphonies before he turned to astronomy.
tossups.r: In 1781, he made this planet the first one ever found with a telescope. For 10 points, name this seventh planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: Gustav Holst’s _The Planets_ calls this planet “the Magician.” It takes about 84 Earth years to circle the Sun, so each of its seasons lasts about 21 years, and as of 2025 it had not yet completed three orbits since its discovery.
tossups.r: This tipped-over planet is named for the Greek god of the sky. For 10 points, name this seventh planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: In 2022, a major report by American planetary scientists named a big orbiter and probe for this planet as NASA’s top priority for its next flagship planetary mission. Such reports are called decadal surveys.
tossups.r: As of 2025, only one spacecraft had visited this planet, in 1986. For 10 points, name this ice giant, the seventh planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: Two small moons named Cordelia and Ophelia herd this planet’s brightest ring, the Epsilon ring, keeping it narrow. Most of this planet’s moons are named for characters from Shakespeare’s plays, but Umbriel and Belinda come from a poem by Alexander Pope.
tossups.r: Its largest moon is Titania. For 10 points, name this seventh planet, which is tipped on its side.

trap.title: Uranus or Neptune?
trap.body: Uranus and Neptune are look-alike blue ice giants, and their clues get mixed up, especially because tugs on Uranus’s orbit led to Neptune’s discovery. Players also blurt out the name of a moon, like Miranda, Titania, or Oberon, when the question wants the planet. The sky god Uranus, the father of Cronus, belongs to mythology questions.
trap.fix: William Herschel, 1781, Bath, Georgium Sidus, a 98-degree tilt, moons named for Shakespeare and Pope characters, and rings found in 1977 mean Uranus. Le Verrier, Adams, Galle, 1846, Triton, the Great Dark Spot, and the fastest winds mean Neptune. If the question says “this planet,” name the planet, not its moon.
